scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a recommendation response that puts basic needs first while arguing against cutting all arts funding; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: When people are struggling to eat or find work, spending on art can seem like a luxury.
Some people recommend that nations should suspend government funding for the arts when many of their citizens are hungry or unemployed.
I agree that basic needs must come first, but I believe cutting all arts funding would be a mistake even in hard times.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why basic needs come first

sentences.text: First, in a serious crisis, meeting people's basic needs must clearly come before funding art.
A government's first duty is to keep its citizens fed, housed, and able to find work.
For example, money spent on a grand new museum would be hard to justify while families nearby go hungry.
This shows that public spending should focus on survival before it focuses on culture.
Citizens who are suffering may rightly resent seeing their taxes spent on art instead of aid.
In an emergency, redirecting funds toward food and jobs is both fair and humane.
To this extent, the recommendation reflects a reasonable sense of priorities.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why not cut all arts funding

sentences.text: Second, however, suspending all arts funding even in hard times would do real harm.
The arts are not a mere luxury but a genuine source of meaning, comfort, and hope.
Consider how music and stories have lifted people's spirits during wars and other times of great hardship.
Such examples show that art can sustain a struggling society rather than waste its resources.
Cutting arts funding also destroys jobs, since many people earn their living through culture.
Once cultural institutions are shut down, they can be very difficult to rebuild later.
Even in hard times, then, some support for the arts remains worthwhile.
In conclusion, a nation in crisis should rightly put food and jobs before funding for the arts.
But cutting all arts funding would needlessly damage the culture and spirit people depend on.
The wiser course is to reduce arts spending if necessary while never abandoning it completely.
